summary: A best current practice guide for people writing Internet standards. It defines the characteristics that make a standard coherent, unambiguous and easy to interpret.

eli5.summary: A how-to guide for writing clear rules, so that no one misunderstands them.

questions: how to write an internet standard
what should a security considerations section contain
what is the liberal conservative rule
what is a summary table in an rfc
subtitle: A checklist of habits that make a protocol specification clear enough for separate teams to build interoperable implementations.

tldr.problem: Unclear specifications are a recognized barrier to interoperable implementations, and past IETF experience showed repeated gaps in security, error handling and options.
tldr.mechanism: The guide lists what a standards-track document should cover (security, protocol description, audience, options, requirement keywords, IANA, management, scaling, stability, internationalization, glossary) and how to present packet diagrams, summary tables and state machines.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 22) used alongside RFC 2223. It does not guarantee interoperability, but it gives authors and reviewers a checklist.

today: RFC 2360 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 22), and the metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It was written to be used with RFC 2223 "or its update".

sections.title: Why a Writing Guide
sections.content:
RFC 2360 is a guide for Internet standards writers. It offers guidelines for writing a standards-track document with clarity, precision and completeness, based on both successful and unsuccessful IETF specification experiences. It is meant to be used with RFC 2223, "Instructions to RFC Authors", or its update.

The goal is to raise the chance that multiple implementations of a protocol will interoperate. The RFC is honest that following the guidelines will not guarantee it, but unclear specifications are a recognized barrier. Implementers, protocol testers (who derive testable statements from the text) and purchasers all benefit from a well-written specification.

For the standards process itself it points to RFC 2026, and for design considerations to RFC 1958. The IESG may require that all or some of the general guidelines appear in a standards-track document, and some guidelines may not apply in certain situations.
sections.eli5: If a recipe is confusing, ten cooks make ten different dishes. This guide helps writers make recipes so clear that every cook makes the same dish.

sections.title: Discussing Security
sections.content:
The guide's longest section is about security. Above all, new protocols and practices must not worsen overall Internet security. Authors must accept that their protocol will be attacked, work out which attacks are possible and describe them in the document. Otherwise they must convincingly argue that attack is not realistic in a specific environment, and restrict the protocol to that environment.

After identifying the risks, authors must formulate and detail a defense, or state the risk the user accepts. Countermeasures may be built into the protocol or rely on external mechanisms. Authors should reuse existing security mechanisms where practical, and when a cryptographic algorithm is used, the protocol should be written so it can be swapped for another algorithm later. The effects of security measures on use and performance should be discussed too.

Security can be discussed in one Security Considerations section or throughout the document. If it is spread through the document, the Security Considerations section must summarize and point to the relevant parts. A section may also discuss the "path not taken": mechanisms that were rejected, and why. Finally, it is no longer acceptable for a Security Considerations section to say only that security was not considered.

Examples the RFC points to include RFC 1350, RFC 1662 and RFC 1939, plus RFC 2316 for more background.
sections.eli5: When you build a treehouse, you should say how someone could break in and how you stop them. Writing "I did not think about it" is not allowed.

sections.title: Protocol Description, Audience and History
sections.content:
A standards-track document must describe the protocol: its purpose, intended functions, the services it provides, and the arena or special circumstances of its use. Authors know why the protocol exists, but readers usually have general networking knowledge rather than expertise in that protocol. The guide recommends the "Protocol Overview" section of RFC 2328 as a good example, and says the description should show the relationship between the parties, for example with typical packet sequences. Algorithms need a detailed description or a citation of readily available references.

The document should also name its target audience, such as designers, implementers, testers, help desk personnel, educators or end users. If there are several audiences, the section for each should be identified.

On the level of detail, concise text is easier to read and reduces conflicts, but may hide the reasoning and cause wrong assumptions. Long text can explain rationale and experience, but requirements become hard to find and one mechanism may be described several times. One suggested approach is to split the document into a concise protocol description and a separate explanatory section, as RFC 1122, RFC 1123 and RFC 2328 do.

As a document moves along the standards track, for example from Proposed to Draft or Draft to Full, it changes. A change log showing what changed from the previous version is required, to help implementers track the changes.

When a standard specifies a new version of an existing protocol, the authors should detail the differences and the rationale, such as implementation experience, changes in technology or user demand.

Authors should also record the basis for contentious decisions. That prevents the same disagreements being reopened after the original people have moved on, and the "why" is as useful to an implementer as the "how". The alternative not taken may have been simpler to implement, so explaining the choice can stop implementers taking nonstandard shortcuts.
sections.eli5:
Say what your game is for and who it is for, and keep the rules short. Put the long story about why you made it in a different chapter.

Keep a diary of what you changed and why you argued about it, so nobody has to have the same argument again next year.

sections.title: Bad Input and the Liberal/Conservative Rule
sections.content:
The standard should describe responses to behavior that is forbidden or outside the specification, because implementers often disagree about the right response. Two approaches are discarding or invoking error-handling mechanisms. If discarding, the disposition may need detailing, for instance treating dropped frames as if never received, or resetting a connection or adjacency state. It should also describe what happens when a critical resource or performance-scaling limit is exceeded.

The guide discusses the rule first stated in RFC 791: "Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send". It urges caution applying it to standards-track protocols, because it has led to vendor conflicts, with the sender blaming the receiver for not being liberal enough and the receiver blaming the sender for not being conservative enough. Authors are therefore obligated to give extensive detail on send and receive behavior, and the guide recommends specifying them separately, with the most detail on reception.

Undefined information or conditions must not cause a network or host failure. Authors should say where the dividing line lies between using as much of a packet as possible and invoking error procedures. For routing protocols, where accepting flawed information can cause network failure, the specification should identify ambiguous packets and mandate rejecting them entirely or define how to recover some information. Its example is a routing update containing more data than the tuple count shows.
sections.eli5: Decide ahead of time what to do when someone passes you a strange note: throw it away, or read the parts that make sense. And never let a strange note crash the whole class.

sections.title: Handling Protocol Options
sections.content:
Many optional features increase implementation complexity and the chance that two implementations cannot interoperate. As a document advances, implementation experience determines whether each option becomes mandatory or stays optional. An option that is not implemented must be removed from the protocol before it reaches draft standard status.

Options should exist only to address a real requirement, for example future extensibility, a particular market, or a constrained network environment. They must not be included to "buy off" a minority opinion, and omitting an option must have no interoperability consequences for the implementation that omits it. One approach is to document options in a separate specification. Either way, the text must discuss the implications of using or not using each option, how options work alongside other protocols, and the default of every option. For security checking options, the default is on.

For mutually exclusive options, the author must state when to implement each, what the effect of the choice is, and what problems may follow, and the choice must have no interoperability consequences between implementations.
sections.eli5: Extra buttons on a toy are fine only if the toy still works with the buttons ignored. Do not add buttons just to make someone stop complaining.

sections.title: Requirement Words, Notation and Other Required Sections
sections.content:
Editors of standards-track documents must use the requirement-level words defined in RFC 2119 (BCP 14) without deviating from their definitions. Capitalization is the accepted norm and can help spot an unintentional or unreasonable requirement. Formal syntax notation, such as the extended BNF in RFC 822 or the ASN.1 subset in RFC 1155, can define complicated data types, but the notation must be referenced, any changes defined, and a parser either available or specifiable. Notation cannot replace a clearly written description.

The guide then lists further topics a standard should cover:

  • IANA considerations: unique parameter values are assigned by the IANA, so authors must coordinate rules for the number space before submitting a draft to the standards track.
  • Network management: discuss how to manage the protocol, and define a MIB in the standard or a companion document, or explain why it is not relevant.
  • Scalability: state limits on the scale of use and on resources used, or explain why not applicable.
  • Network stability: discuss topology and convergence behavior, troublesome topologies and destabilizing events. This applies to application protocols too.
  • Internationalization: conform to BCP 18, RFC 2277.
  • Glossary: every standards-track RFC should have one, defining new words at first use and in a glossary section, with RFC 1983 as the reference for common terms.
sections.eli5: Use the special words MUST and SHOULD exactly as defined, ask the number-keeper before you hand out numbers, say how to look after it, and explain any new words.

sections.title: Diagrams, Summary Tables and State Machines
sections.content:
The guide's specific advice covers three presentation tools.

Packet diagrams are preferred as a sequence of long words in network byte order, each word horizontal with bit numbering at the top (the RFC shows a 32-bit-wide layout). For strongly byte-aligned packets, use a byte-wide format, with broken boxes for variable-length fields.

Summary tables help with specifications that run a hundred pages or more by itemizing what is mandatory, optional or prohibited. They have at least four columns: Protocol Feature, Section Reference, Status, and References/Footnotes. Suggested status codes are M, MN, O, S, SN and X. RFC 1122 and RFC 1123 are examples.

State machines define the variables and events that cause transitions and the actions that result. They are never to replace the detailed text, and the specification takes precedence in a conflict. They can be shown as diagrams, as tables (events listed vertically, states horizontally, entries in the form action/new state, as in RFC 1661) or as time lines, with the two machines on either side and time progressing downward.
sections.eli5: Draw the pieces of a message as boxes in a row, make a chart saying which rules are a must or a maybe, and show how a machine hops from one state to the next.

sections.title: The Document Checklist
sections.content:
Section 4 turns the guidance into a checklist of questions an author or reviewer can ask. The questions include:

  • Does it identify security risks, provide countermeasures and detail their effects?
  • Does it explain the purpose, intended functions and services, and how it relates to existing protocols?
  • Does it consider scaling and stability, and are number assignments coordinated with the IANA?
  • Does it discuss management and define a MIB, and is a target audience defined?
  • Is there a change log, and are differences from previous versions described?
  • Does it separate explanation from requirements, and identify one description as binding if there are several?
  • How many options are there, are they split into classes, and have all combinations been checked for incompatibility?
  • Does it use the requirement key words, follow internationalization policy and define altered terms in a glossary?
sections.eli5: It ends with a to-do list. Before you hand in your rules, tick off every question to be sure you did not forget anything.
